content: The document titled Guidelines for the Screening, Care, and Treatment of Persons with Hepatitis C Infection was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in April 2014. It provides comprehensive recommendations for the management of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, including its prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. The guidelines are intended to support policymakers, government officials, and healthcare providers, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, in developing effective programs for HCV care. Hepatitis C is a significant global health issue, with over 185 million people infected worldwide and approximately 350,000 deaths annually. Chronic HCV infection can lead to severe complications, including liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, in about one-third of those affected. Despite the high prevalence, many individuals remain unaware of their infection, and access to treatment is limited in many regions. The guidelines emphasize that hepatitis C differs from other chronic viral infections, such as HIV, because it is curable with appropriate treatment. Advances in HCV therapeutics have led to the development of highly effective medications, with cure rates exceeding 90% in many cases. These newer treatments are also effective against previously difficult-to-treat HCV genotypes. Currently available treatments for HCV include pegylated and standard interferon-alpha (IFN), ribavirin (RBV), protease inhibitors (such as boceprevir, telaprevir, and simeprevir), and the NS5B nucleotide polymerase inhibitor sofosbuvir. The field of HCV treatment is rapidly evolving, with additional antiviral compounds expected to be licensed in the near future. The guidelines include recommendations for all medicines approved as of December 2013 and will be updated periodically as new treatments become available. The development of these guidelines followed the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2012) and utilized the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology. This approach ensures a systematic and evidence-based process for defining research questions, conducting systematic reviews, and assessing the quality of evidence. The guidelines aim to expand clinical services for HCV patients by providing key recommendations and addressing considerations for implementation. They serve as a framework for improving access to care and treatment, particularly in resource-limited settings, and highlight the importance of integrating HCV management into broader healthcare systems. The document also acknowledges the contributions of numerous experts, organizations, and institutions involved in its development. It includes a glossary of terms, a list of abbreviations, and appendices with detailed technical information, such as systematic reviews, evidence summaries, and decision-making tables. The guidelines are a critical resource for addressing the global burden of hepatitis C and improving outcomes for affected individuals.
